title: Ukraine F-16 Update: Jets From Belgium, Maintenance Concerns And Block 70/72 fighters
body: Belgium is set to deliver its first three F-16AM/BM fighters to Ukraine following a several-year delay, as Kyiv also discusses with Lockheed Martin about adopting the latest variant of the fighter jet. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy announced on Sept. 29, 2026, that Belgium will begin the transfer of its elderly F-16AM/BM Fighting Falcons to Ukraine by the end ‌of the year. The first delivery will see three aircraft sent, with the rest of the 30 promised aircraft being delivered as Belgium equips itself with F-35A Lightning IIs bought directly from the United States. The promised delivery follows a long delay, with the aircraft originally pledged in May 2024 to be delivered towards the end of the year and up until 2028. Unlike the Dutch and Norwegian F-16 deliveries, these transfers were held up by the slow roll out of Belgium’s F-35s, as the country was not willing to part with its combat aircraft until it had at least some replacements in service. To this date, only seven F-35s have been delivered to Belgium, of which three aircraft were delivered on Sept. 24 . Delivery of Belgium’s first four F-35s from the United States. They arrived in Belgium landing at Florennes Air Base in October 2025. | Source: Belgian Ministry of Defence Making the announcement, President Zelenskyy emphasised the importance of the deliveries of new kit to Ukraine to combat the Russian threat, with the expedited delivery of “F-16 ammunition from Belgium and other countries, including Spain” being instrumental to Ukraine’s air defence. These deliveries likely included a number of AIM-120 AMRAAM, AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds which are instrumental in the Ukrainian Air Force’s (UkrAF) defensive counter air campaign, shooting down large numbers of Russian drones and cruise missiles. The F-16s have also recently been augmented with the supply of the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) guided rockets, which allow Ukrainian fighters to shoot down Russian drones at a far cheaper cost than the use of a normal missile. There is an important agreement with Belgium on the transfer of three F-16 fighter jets by the end of this year. We will work to receive these aircraft through an accelerated procedure. We have already received urgent deliveries of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and other… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 29, 2026 On this point, during a meeting with Lockheed Martin representatives to discuss Ukraine’s future fighter capabilities, the Commander of the Ukrainian Air Force, Lieutenant General Anatolii Kryvonozhko, announced that F-16 pilots have shot down “over 3,150 enemy aerial targets which include 666 cruise missiles and an estimated 2,500 drones of various types.” The F-16 is a potent counter cruise missile and drone platform, having the speed to chase them down and destroy them before they impact civilian areas. The F-16 has also been an effective close air support platform, conducting “650 airstrikes” against the ground forces of the Russian Federation. The principle air-to-ground munitions employed by Ukrainian F-16s appear to be the GBU-39 Small Diameter Bombs (SDB). A single jet can carry up to eight of the 250 lb munitions without having to renounce to drop tanks and air-to-air munitions. Ukraine also employs several variants of the Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM). This weapon comes in a number of different weight classes, with 500 lb and 1000 lb variants seen in use in Ukraine, and can be equipped with a glide kit or a rocket kit to extend the range, however they have not yet been photographed on Ukrainian F-16s. Ukrainian F-16 pilots have shot down over 3,150 enemy aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones of various types, and have also carried out more than 650 airstrikes against enemy ground targets. This was reported by the Commander of the Ukrainian Air… pic.twitter.com/A9136JeJkF — MilitaryNewsUA (@front_ukrainian) September 29, 2026 The F-16s and their Ukrainian pilots have proven themselves to be extremely effective since their introduction with the aircraft, now forming the bedrock of the current and future Ukrainian fighter force. However, the models delivered were all original A and B variant F-16s that were built in the 1970s and 1980s, making them similar in age to their former ex-Soviet fleet of aircraft. These fighters did receive a midlife update to extend their service lives and to give them more advanced air-to-air and air-to-ground capabilities. However, they are reaching the end of their useful service lives due to airframe fatigue and they are facing increasing maintenance demands after intensive use in the Russo-Ukrainian War. Belgian Air Component F-16AM fighter jet at RAF Waddington for Exercise COBRA WARRIOR in 2023. This fleet is transiting over to the F-35 as the air force modernises itself. | Source: Crown copyright 2023/Sgt Nicholas Howe RAF It was reported by the Wall Street Journal that maintenance of these aircraft is fast becoming an issue with an unnamed source stating that “more than half of Ukraine’s F-16s are currently in maintenance limbo” and that “Kyiv will exhaust the rest by the end of the year.” This is a worrying development if confirmed, as the F-16 is essential for Ukraine’s continued defence of its skies. Reportedly, this is due to delays at Sabena Aerospace Engineering, a Belgian company that is responsible for the long term maintenance of the F-16s used by Ukraine. Retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery stated that the aircraft need to undergo regular phase inspections every 300 hours, which should take weeks. However, in Belgium it’s “taking as long as 40 weeks,” delaying maintenance and leaving aircraft unable to fly. More than half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets are currently not operational due to maintenance delays in Belgium – WSJ A significant number of the fighter jets remain grounded due to a lack of spare parts and the need for more frequent repairs following intensive use. Given the… pic.twitter.com/9tWkGDSb8F — Jürgen Nauditt (@jurgen_nauditt) September 30, 2026 Details on this issue are scarce, but they paint a worrying picture for the UkrAF which has already undergone years of degradation due to the war. It is hoped that the integration of further aircraft into the force would alleviate some of these maintenance issues, allowing for a large pool of spare aircraft, and the possible maintenance of the jets in Ukraine itself. The importance of the F-16 to Ukraine’s current and future air force needs is likely what led to the meeting between Ukrainian representatives and Lockheed Martin to explore the possibility of supplying Ukraine with the far more advanced F-16 Block 70/72 , which uses capabilities derived from the F-22 and F-35 programmes. The introduction of newer jets could ease the maintenance burden as these aircraft would be fresh and infinitely more capable than their forefathers. Belgian Air Component F-16BM fighter jet at RAF Fairford for the Royal International Air Tattoo in 2024. This two seater was joined by F-16s from across the world to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the jet. | Source: James Gray Conor McGuire, Lockheed’s F-16 capability development lead, praised the work of Ukrainian pilots and ground crews and expressed his intention to help improve the aircraft Ukraine already operates. Whether this could be through further upgrades to the F-16AM/BM fleet or in the provision of further maintenance infrastructure is currently speculation. Ukraine’s Ex-Soviet Force Ukraine started the war with a mixed fleet of ex-Soviet aircraft which were already ageing out at the start of the conflict. Its mainstay air-to-air fighters in 2022 consisted of a force of around 70 MiG-29 Fulcrums and 34 Su-27 Flanker jet fighters, which bore a significant brunt of the early air war. When the Ukrainian ground based air defences had to be displaced during the opening days, it was up to these aircraft and their pilots to absorb the might of Russia’s air power. The MiG-29 and Su-27 fleets suffered several losses during those opening days, but they managed to stem the Russian tide long enough for the ground based air defences to secure the skies over Ukraine. Since then, these fleets have been upgraded to employ western missiles and bombs, including the AGM-88 High Speed Anti-Radiation Missile (HARM), which is used to suppress Russia’s air defence systems, as well as the 1,000 lb GBU-62 JDAM-ER and the 500 lb GBU-39B Small Diameter Bomb precision glide bombs. A MiG-29 of the 114th Tactical Aviation Brigade pulls a high speed manoeuvre. The leading edges of the wings and the horizontal stabilisers are painted in Ukrainian blue and yellow to ease identification during combat and prevent friendly fire at low level. | Source: Ukrainian Air Force Their primary role however remained air defence, with these aircraft maintaining the defensive counter air mission against missiles and drones until the introduction of the F-16. The actions of the 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade, who flew MiG-29s over Kyiv during the early days of the war, birthed the legend of the ‘ Ghost of Kyiv ’, the name of which was later awarded to them in 2024 via presidential decree. There have been a number of attrition replacements for Ukraine’s MiG-29 fleet, including 13 from Slovakia , 14 from Poland , along with a number of spare parts that allowed Ukraine to reactivate some of its stored fighters as well as three that Azerbaijan had in Ukraine for maintenance. However, losses have been heavy, with 39 aircraft visually confirmed damaged or destroyed, leaving the MiG-29 fleet significantly depleted over time. Colonel Oleksandr Oksanchenko’s Su-27 that he flew during the Royal International Air Tattoo in 2019. | Source: James Gray The Su-27 has not received any attrition replacements, with 20 confirmed lost over the course of the fighting. This included the tragic loss of Colonel Oleksandr Oksanchenko ‘ The Grey Wolf ’, Ukraine’s principal Su-27 display pilot, who was killed in combat on Feb. 25, 2022. His loss was sorely felt in the air show community, with the Royal International Air Tattoo dedicating a memorial to him at the show that same year. The memorial to the fallen pilot in 2022. His loss, amongst so many, was sorely felt. | Source: James Gray Ukraine’s primary air-to-ground aircraft at the war’s start were the 14 or so Su-24 Fencer and the 30 odd Su-25 Frogfoots which have also played key parts in the war to date. The Fencer fleet was essential early in the war to provide close air support and interdiction against Russian forces that landed at the Hostomel airport in 2022. Their attack here helped to block the runway that the Russian paratroopers of the VDV were going to use to bring in reinforcements by air, which gave the Ukrainian units of the National Guard the time to counter attack and contain the Russian landing. The actions here prevented the loss of Kyiv and allowed the country to stay in the fight for the long term. Ukrainian Air Force Su-24M Fencer with underwing Storm Shadow missiles from the front. | Source: Vladyslav Demyanenko/Ukrainian Air Force The Su-24 was also the aircraft chosen to carry the British, French and Italian donated Storm Shadow and SCALP-EG air launched cruise missiles (ALCMs), which have proven devastating against Russian supply depots, bridges and naval forces. Parts from the Panavia Tornado were bolted on to the airframe to allow for the missile to be integrated, allowing it to carry the weapon into combat. Due to this mission set, losses have been lighter than during the early war, as the Storm Shadow has a long stand-off launch distance, enabling the Su-24 to stay out of Russia’s air defences. However, the fleet has still lost 22 airframes in total, along with many of their pilots. Keen eyed observers will see that losses for the Su-24 are higher than their initial fleet total. This is thanks to the maintainers and engineers who were able to bring back a significant number of aircraft from storage, giving them a new lease of life to fight the invasion. Rare footage of the release of French guided aerial bombs AASM Hammer from the board of a Ukrainian Su-25 attack aircraft. pic.twitter.com/J7lFfzA0dr — MilitaryNewsUA (@front_ukrainian) April 11, 2026 Likewise, the Su-25 has been Ukraine’s primary close air support weapon, delivering volleys of unguided rockets at long distance early in the war due to heavy losses . The supply of Soviet munitions dwindled over time due to a lack of resupply, and so the Su-25 took more of a backseat to the MiG-29 in the ground attack role. However, the fleet was significantly augmented with deliveries of French AASM Hammer bombs which gave the Frogfoot the stand off distance it needed to get back into the fight. Losses have still been unfortunately high, with 22 aircraft lost over the last five years of war, significantly degrading the fleet. The ex-Soviet force of fighter planes and their pilots have soldiered on far longer than anyone had expected them to when the war started in 2022. However, it is the assistance of NATO and Ukraine’s Western allies that will enable the UkrAF to develop into the future. The Future Fighter Fleet The first F-16s entered Ukrainian airspace in August 2024, following extensive training programs abroad in multiple European partner nations as well as the United States. Jointly,they set up the European F-16 Training Center (EFTC) at the 86th Air Base in Fetești, Romania, which serves to train Ukrainian and Romanian pilots on the platform. Three Ukrainian F-16s flying in formation together, each is equipped for an air-to-air engagement, carrying AIM-120 AMRAAMs and AIM-9 Sidewinders, likely for counter drone missions. | Source: Ukrainian Air Force With this and several other training programmes in place, F-16AM/BM aircraft were then donated by Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, and soon to be Belgium, to sustain the UkrAF. According to retired USAF pilot Lt. Gen. David Deptula , Ukraine’s F-16s now fly “80 percent” of all Ukrainian combat sorties, marking a significant change in the makeup of the overall fighter force. Even with the maintenance problems already discussed above, the F-16, being a Western jet, has more available spares than the ex-Soviet fleet, with the majority of spare parts being controlled by the Russian Federation. Ukraine currently has an estimated 39 F-16s in service, so far having lost five to attrition over the last few years, but it is expected to raise to a maximum of 80 aircraft once deliveries from Denmark and Belgium are completed. At that point, the F-16 will be the most numerous fighter in Ukrainian service. Cockpit photo from a Ukrainian Air Force F-16 Sept. 10, 2026, while defending against a Russian mass air attack. Off the aircraft’s starboard side, a Russian jet-powered Geran one-way attack drone can be seen falling from the sky, trailing smoke, having been shot down by the Ukrainian pilot—his third gun kill of the sortie, using the F-16’s 20mm cannon. | Source: Official Ukrainian Air Force Tragically, Ukrainian MiG-29 pilot Captain Andrii Pilshchykov ‘Juice’, who played a key role in advocating for the delivery of F-16s to Ukraine, was killed in a training exercise in August 2023. Following his initial wartime service, he spent months giving interviews to Western media and even traveled to the U.S. to meet and convince American lawmakers to enable the donation of the fighters to Ukraine. He was very much the public face of the campaign to see Ukrainian pilots in F-16s and their current impact on the war is in no small part due to his efforts. A message from ‘Juice’ — the Ukrainian MiG-29 pilot I interviewed a few weeks ago. Story: https://t.co/t4fRmqaQXI https://t.co/zOpPzN2cYI — Nolan Peterson (@nolanwpeterson) April 16, 2022 Alongside the F-16, Ukraine has also received six Mirage 2000-5 fighter jets from France, with one lost to attrition quite soon after their initial delivery. These aircraft also allow for the employment of SCALP-EG ALCMs, taking some of the strain off the dwindling Su-24 force. It is expected that France will send more to Ukraine as it retires its current fleet, with between 12 and 20 aircraft expected to be delivered over the coming years. A Ukrainian Mirage 2000 takes off carrying Magic 2 air-to-air missiles for air defence purposes. | Source: Ukrainian Air Force This fleet acts more as an interim option before 16 Dassault Rafales can be delivered to the country, following an announcement made by French President Macron in July this year. The first four aircraft will be delivered following completion of their pilots training which is starting this year. It is still unknown if these will be new build fighters, or more likely aircraft from existing French stocks, though they are part of a purchase that aims to see 100 Rafales in Ukrainian colours . Unlike the donated Mirages, these aircraft are paid for by the Ukraine Support Loan and will give the Ukrainians a new advantage over their Russian opponent with the introduction of the Meteor missile to the battlefield. The Rafale will be the premier fighter of the future UkrAF , but it will not be alone. Up to 16 Gripen C/Ds are expected to be donated to Ukraine in early 2027, coming directly from the Swedish Air Force. These aircraft will then be joined by a further 20 Gripen E/F fighters, which have a capability comparable to the Rafale but with a significantly improved rough strip performance. Sweden will donate 16 Gripen C/D fighters to Ukraine, with deliveries starting early next year. Ukraine will additionally purchase 20x Gripen E fighters, with deliveries starting in 2030. Sweden will additionally provide maintenance and training support. pic.twitter.com/y748IDg1Bq — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) May 28, 2026 The final tally of expected aircraft will be around 150 aircraft, rising to around 300 if Ukraine’s aspirational orders of 100 Rafales and 100 Gripen Es come to fruition. Either way, the added aircraft more than make up for the losses in material incurred so far during the war and will give Ukraine an advantage over Russia in the air for the very first time. It is still a long road until Ukraine receives all its fighters, and the logistical nightmare that such a diverse fleet represents will be a tough manage for a force already operating six types of frontline aircraft. The F-16 Block 70/72 Given the progress made in F-16 training, UkrAF performance and the logistical challenges that introducing a new aircraft into service becomes, Ukraine is also exploring a possible pivot to newer block models of the aircraft. The F-16 training centre is a long term investment that could be greatly improved upon with the acquisition of 4.5 generation F-16s, which have capabilities similar to Gripen and Rafale, but in a package that Ukraine is already using en masse. Finally, after years of delay, the first of the 66 new F-16V Block 70s for the Taiwanese Air Force has been delivered. Packing an AESA radar, modern avionics, and a much nastier electronic warfare suite, this latest Viper is a very different beast from the F-16 that first took to… pic.twitter.com/zcXHlmydzT — Air Power (@RealAirPower1) August 29, 2026 The F-16 Block 70/72, or F-16V in the case of existing aircraft upgraded to the new standard, is the most modern variant of the aircraft, representing both new builds directly from Lockheed Martin as well as upgrade packages for older aircraft. The variant uses an advanced APG-83 AESA radar, a massive improvement over the older mechanically scanned arrays that Ukraine currently uses, having better range, better electronic warfare capabilities and better data links. The radar leverages hardware and software commonality with F-22 and F-35 AESA radars, giving it some of the benefits of a 5th generation aircraft. The aircraft utilises a modernized cockpit to allow for better systems integration, and vastly improved avionics. Some versions come with conformal fuel tanks to improve the aircraft’s baseline range, which could drastically improve the survivability of the aircraft on the ground, operating further away from the front. These capabilities could be added onto existing F-16s through a modification programme similar to that undergone by Taiwan’s F-16 force , but it would require significant assistance from the United States. Relations between Ukraine and the U.S. are at a warmer point than they were the previous year, with Ukraine having reached an agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump for the production of the missiles used in Patriot air defence systems. The Block 70/72 variants would be a significant boon to the UkrAF, but only time will tell if the force is able to acquire them.

title: Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address
body: MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, Va.— Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide drive to field autonomous systems, as the Pentagon’s takes a bullish approach towards artificial intelligence and drone warfare. He also unveiled five other initiatives during what he promised will become an annual “State of the Force” address here Sept. 30. Hegseth plans to launch the Autonomous Warfare Command within a year as a combatant command endowed with “service-like authorities, built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” he said. Its portfolio will include drones, artificial intelligence, and command and control systems. Hegseth also announced the creation of a new program office, led by a two-star officer, to ensure military installations can generate their own power to isolate themselves from attacks on public grids. Bases in the homeland are increasingly seen as possibly contested environments where the U.S. military must be able to operate while under threat in a age of increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and so-called hybrid warfare activities by America’s adversaries. And he confirmed plans to slash the total number of generals and admirals across the military by 20 percent, a move Air & Space Forces Magazine and other outlets had reported would be part of Hegseth’s speech. Other initiatives include: A new group, dubbed “Project Meridian,” to study the future of warfare led by tech leaders Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, who were in attendance. An initiative, called the “Next Great American Base,” to build a new military installation to host 15,000-25,000 service members. Hegseth said governors and adjutant generals from every state will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch locations. The creation of five new corps of cadets at Hillsdale College, Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Mississippi State University, and Tuskegee University, which will all be given priority in officer commissioning. A new “Office of Religious Affairs” reporting directly to the Secretary of Defense to give chaplains better access to senior leadership. Exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of senior officers and enlisted from commands across the globe to Quantico for an address outlining his vision for the U.S. military, he spoke this time to an audience of around 600 E-6 enlisted members and O-3 officers, who the Pentagon said were selected by their units for their performance and leadership potential. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force Gen. Dan Caine briefly addressed the crowd and introduced Hegseth. Autonomy The new Autonomous Warfare Command will drive the design, development, and fielding of autonomous and semi-autonomous capabilities and systems. “The autonomous and robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades,” Hegseth said. “Civilian leaders can provide direction and urgency, but lasting change must be anchored in military command structures and operationalized by leaders across our joint force.” The Pentagon is already leaning heavily into autonomy, and the new command is designed to significantly accelerate that effort. Lawmakers in the Senate had proposed the creation of such a combatant command during deliberations for the 2027 defense policy bill. The measure cleared the committee, but the bill is still pending. To be authorized, the House would also have to approve the measure. It is not yet clear how the new four-star command will be structured, who will lead it, or how it will work with the autonomy efforts already underway within the different services. In a memo , Hegseth wrote the Pentagon plans to work with Congress to stand up the command by October 1, 2027, a year on from the announcement. Hegseth said it will start with an interim step, dubbed “Project Agincourt,” named for the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Project Agincourt will draw from existing efforts like the Defense Innovation Unit and the Drone Dominance program, Hegseth said, and pair “operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units.” Project Agincourt will be guided by DIU director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser, the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School. Creating Autonomous Warfare Command will take place “over the course of several months,” Hegseth said. The Air Force and Navy are already developing Collaborative Combat Aircraft: semi-autonomous drones designed to work alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force is also pursuing a lower-cost intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drone with autonomous capabilities under its Massed Modular Aircraft program, and the Navy is working to field an unmanned tanker drone, the MQ-25. The growth of autonomomy and the Penatagon’s future plans to harvest technology with its new command represent the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” Hegseth said. “Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he added, using an acronym for so-called super intelligence, President Donald Trump’s favored term for AI. At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference earlier this month, Air Force leadership made it clear they see autonomous systems as central to the service’s future. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference that while true autonomous aircraft are a “few years off,” the service is leaning heavily into autonomy in its current future Force Design model. “The FQ-42 and the FQ-44 [Collaborative Combat Aircraft] are autonomous fighters, and then we’re going to have perhaps other platforms that are autonomous, where you don’t actually need a crew to do a fighter mission,” Wilsbach said during a session with reporters. “You just send the aircraft off, and it does its mission because it’s automated.” The Pentagon has deployed uncrewed surface vessels operationally in the Middle East for a few years for maritime surveillance. This summer, a U.S. Navy drone boat was even able to rescue two downed Army Apache pilots near the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Southern Command, which has been conducting strikes on boats suspected of smuggling drugs for over a year, recently established an autonomous warfare branch that will employ its own uncrewed vessels and aerial intelligence-gathering platforms. On the southern border, the U.S. military is now using 10 uncrewed surface vessels to patrol the Rio Grande River, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs M. Roosevelt Ditlevson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview. “We’re moving into next-generation tools here that we’re going to employ to make sure that we hold these narcoterrorists at bay,” Ditlevson said, referring to the drug smugglers. “I’m very excited about what is going to happen in the autonomy space and how we’re going to employ these different systems.” But the Pentagon is automating more than aircraft, ships, and vehicles. The Pentagon’s Maven Smart System has become a key tool for the U.S. military, a system aggregating sensors, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and command and control as part of the targeting process. Maven is used for operations ranging from targeting assistance in the Middle East to, more recently, counter-drone and anti-smuggling efforts on the southern border. Ditlevson said AI, through Maven, will also feed into the Pentagon’s sweeping Golden Dome missile defense shield. “Maven Smart System is going to feed into the Golden Dome picture,” he said. At the border, the Defense Department also uses autonomy software called Fortress, an adaptation of Anduril’s Lattice, which integrates data and sensors using AI. “All of our systems must be compatible with Maven Smart System,” Ditlevson said. “Everything that we have, that data needs to be integrated into Maven and into Lattice.” To support all these new autonomous systems, Hegseth said, each military service will phase in new military occupational specialties for autonomy. “We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters,” he said. Fortress America Hegseth also said the Pentagon is creating a new initiative called “Fortress America” to ensure military installations are able to generate their own power. The Pentagon has been working on building nuclear microreactors at key U.S. bases in the homeland and has previously said it plans to field a nuclear reactor at a military base by September 2028. The Air Force in particular is working on a microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, with plans to build more at other bases in the coming years. The service has also explored using alternate power sources like solar panels, geothermal plants, and more to create so-called “ microgirds ” for bases so they’re not entirely reliant on local civilian power grids. The drive to give bases their own energy sources is driven by concerns that adversaries may target critical infrastructure, around 80 percent of which is currently in the commercial sector, to kneecap the military’s ability to generate forces. The Pentagon chief referred to the program as “nation’s insurance policy” in a memo directing the establishment of Fortress America. Hegseth is also slashing the number of general and flag officers , cutting billets by 20 percent. That doubles down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy. “The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said. “And I know because I directed it that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent. So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.” Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today. The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs. The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and has plans to continue to grow that number. A year ago, most senior military leaders gave stoic reactions during politically charged speeches from Hegseth and Trump, keeping with the military’s apolitical tradition. The troops at this year’s addres gave Hegseth a more vocal reception, particularly during his reference to Musk, Luckey, and Gingrich, and Hegseth exited to applause from the troops, though service members appeared to avoid visual reactions to Hegseth’s more ideological comments. Attendees were separated by branch, and were given a “War Department Field Manual,” a collection speeches by Hegseth with a forward written by Trump. Earlier in the day, the service members in attendance participated in a physical training session with Hegseth on the grounds of the Pentagon. title: Where Are The Aircraft Carriers?: September 30, 2026
body: On a hazy, humid Sunday morning, just before 9:30 a.m. local time, the USS Theodore Roosevelt sailed out of San Diego Bay for a much-anticipated but little-advertised deployment. The Nimitz class flagship of Carrier Strike Group 9 (CSG-9), nicknamed “The Big Stick,” departed on September 27 and is expected to head to the Middle East to relieve one of the two carriers on station supporting operations against Iran, according to USNI News . As is common with deployments from the West Coast, the departure was not announced by the Navy publicly, although there were several unconfirmed claims on social media that highlighted the impending cruise. The three-ship Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG), packed with thousands of Marines who specialize in expeditionary operations, followed Roosevelt’s path out of the harbor the next day . While the Makin Island ARGs ultimate destination is unclear, the Boxer ARG, currently operating in the Middle East, left the United States on March 18 and is due for relief. In This Article Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group Deploys, Reportedly Bound For The Middle East Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group Also Deploys, Destination Unknown Abraham Lincoln Days Away From Well-Deserved Homecoming Growler Mishap On Dwight D. Eisenhower Reports Surface That George H.W. Bush Is Headed To Thailand For A Port Call Big Deck Fleet At A Glance SHOW 3 MORE Here’s TWZ’s weekly carrier tracker monitoring America’s flattop fleet, including deployed CSGs and ARGs, using publicly available open-source information. Check out last week’s report here . TWZ/IAN ELLIS-JONES Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group Deploys, Reportedly Bound For The Middle East USS Theodore Roosevelt keyed her Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponder on at 9:10 a.m. Pacific Daylight Time on September 27, broadcasting her precise position publicly via MarineTraffic , and got underway less than 20 minutes later with the help of a few tugs. The supercarrier steamed past Point Loma at seven knots before sailing west and picking up speed, topping 24 knots, then made a hard turn south and stopped transmitting on AIS roughly three hours after departing. She briefly flipped AIS back on again, 55 nautical miles southwest of her previous location, but has been dark since. USS Theodore Roosevelt’s transit leaving San Diego. Source: MarineTraffic/KPLER (Reprinted with permission) Three guided-missile destroyers, USS Paul Hamilton , USS Decatur , and USS Carl M. Levin , are part of CSG-9 and will escort the flattop, TWZ has learned. Rounding out the five-ship CSG is Ticonderoga class guided-missile cruiser USS Chosin , which will serve as the Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) commander for the CSG. The IAMD warfare commander is responsible for coordinating air defense for the entire strike group − a vital role since Roosevelt will be entering an active combat zone. Tico cruisers have 122 Vertical Launch System (VLS) cells, more than the 90 to 96 that Arleigh Burke destroyers are equipped with, and are being retired without a comparable cruiser lined up to replace the aging fleet; however, the newest Flight III Burke destroyers will take on the air warfare commander role. The carrier has embarked, or is in the process of taking on , Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 11 off the West Coast before beginning the long journey toward the Western Pacific. CVW 11 includes a squadron of stealthy fifth-generation F-35C Lightning IIs, in addition to three squadrons of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and one of EA-18G Growlers. Support squadrons of E-2D Hawkeyes, MH-60R Seahawks, and MH-60S Seahawks are also aboard, as well as a detachment of CMV-22B Ospreys. Flight deck of USS Theodore Roosevelt. U.S. Navy photo MH-60S Sea Hawk on USS Theodore Roosevelt. U.S. Navy photo USNI News was the first outlet to confirm the deployment and suggests the CSG is headed to the Middle East. “The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group is expected to move to U.S. Central Command to relieve the Japan-based USS George Washington (CVN-73),” they wrote in a report published on Monday. In response to a request to confirm the deployment, a Navy official told TWZ , “The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group is underway conducting routine operations in the U.S. 3rd Fleet area of operations. U.S. 3rd Fleet leads naval forces in the region and provides the realistic, relevant training necessary to execute our Navy’s role across the full spectrum of military operations – from combat operations to humanitarian assistance and disaster response. U.S. 3rd Fleet works together with allies and partners to advance freedom of navigation and overflight, the rule of law, and other principles that underpin security for the region.” The underway was live-streamed on San Diego Web Cam , which had a few hundred viewers at the peak. TWZ was monitoring the feed at the time after rumors surfaced that a departure was imminent. Notably, Sailors were not spotted manning the rails, which is usually an easy tell that a warship is deploying rather than training. However, several public posts on social media by individual Sailors, as well as their friends and family, pointed to the ship heading on its long-awaited cruise. Video: @SanDiegoWebCam/YouTube Roosevelt has been preparing for the cruise for the better part of a year. The CSG last deployed from January 11 to October 15, 2024, to the U.S. 5th and 7th Fleet areas of responsibility (AOR) in support of Operation Prosperity Guardian . After arriving back home nearly two years ago, the carrier underwent an eight-month Planned Incremental Availability (PIA). Following the PIA, she completed flight deck certification and carrier qualifications from July 23 to July 29, 2025. In 2026, the carrier conducted Composite Unit Training Exercise (COMPTUEX) from April 14 to May 15, and then steamed to Hawaii for the large-scale, biennial Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC) exercise from June 24 to July 28. Most recently, Roosevelt completed a brief pierside availability prior to deploying, as TWZ first reported . In February, Vice Adm. Brendan McLane told reporters at WEST 2026 that a medium unmanned surface vessel (MUSV) would deploy with the strike group for the first time. During COMPTUEX and RIMPAC, the Roosevelt CSG drilled alongside Leidos’ MUSV Seahawk, which TWZ was the first to report . We asked the Navy to confirm whether an MUSV would accompany the group, but have not received a response. As of publication, Seahawk was still pierside in San Diego, and it’s unclear if the drone boat will operate with the CSG or remain in San Diego. Transit of USS Theodore Roosevelt and MUSV Seahawk during COMPTUEX training. Source: MarineTraffic/KPLER (Reprinted with permission) and DVIDS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group Also Deploys, Destination Unknown The three-ship Makin Island ARG, with the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU) embarked, got underway for a deployment on September 28, a Navy official also confirmed to USNI News . In addition to the flagship Wasp class amphibious assault ship (LHD), USS Makin Island , two San Antonio class amphibious transport dock ships (LPD), USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage , left on the same day and round out the expeditionary group. Video: @SanDiegoWebCam/YouTube No destination has been formally announced. However, there is an obvious candidate for relief: the Boxer ARG. Currently on station in the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) AOR supporting blockade and interdiction operations in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, the group has been deployed since mid-March. The amphibious fleet is notorious for experiencing maintenance issues , and these ships have been pushed hard without a port call in months. Amphibious ships move slower than carriers, and if CENTCOM turns out to be the final destination, the Makin Island ARG would have to hustle to arrive before November. Makin Island embarks short takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) F-35B Lightning IIs, assigned to the “Wake Island Avengers” of Marine Fighter Attack Squadron (VMFA) 211, and MV-22B Ospreys with Marine Medium Tiltrotor Squadron (VMM) 364 (Reinforced). The Bravos recently conducted a simulated airstrike off the coast of California. 13th MEU conducts a simulated airstrike aboard USS Makin Island (LHD 8) off the coast of California. U.S. Navy video Abraham Lincoln Days Away From Well-Deserved Homecoming Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao flew out to the flight deck of USS Abraham Lincoln as she was sailing eastbound in the Hawaiian Islands operating area, en route to her homeport in San Diego. “Today, our warfighters aboard USS Abraham Lincoln demonstrated the overwhelming capacity and capability that they brought to bear on our adversaries for the last 10 months,” he wrote in a post on Sunday. USS Abraham Lincoln transiting in the U.S. 7th Fleet AOR. U.S. Navy photo USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. , a destroyer that escorted Lincoln throughout the 10-month deployment, peeled off and moored at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on Monday. “Over the course of 300 days, Frank E. Petersen Jr.’s crew conducted 45 replenishments-at-sea, sailed over 85,000 nautical miles, safely transferred over 7,544,486 gallons of F-76 fuel and 175,288 gallons of JP-5 fuel, and completed 1,094 hours of flight quarters,” according to a press release . The statement also confirmed that the warship served as IAMD commander for the group. The destroyer defended against more than 100 missile and drone attacks, Stars and Stripes recently reported . Petersen Jr. and USS Michael Murphy became the first U.S. warships to transit the Strait of Hormuz since the war began when they entered the Persian Gulf in April in support of mine-clearance efforts. USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. returns to Pearl Harbor. U.S. Navy photo Lincoln is now 314 days into her deployment and less than two weeks shy of surpassing the 326-day record USS Gerald R. Ford set in May. Approximately 2,000 nautical miles separate Hawaii from Naval Air Station North Island, but assuming a straight shot, it does not appear Lincoln will break the record. Growler Mishap On Dwight D. Eisenhower Two crew members from an EA-18G Growler embarked on the aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower ( Ike ) were rescued after ejecting due to an arresting gear failure , the Navy announced in a statement . The incident took place on Monday around 6:18 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time as the vessel was underway off the coast of Virginia. The aviators, assigned to the “Zappers” of Electronic Attack Squadron (VAQ) 130 and attached to CVW 3, “safely returned to the ship and are being evaluated by medical personnel,” according to the release. The “Dusty Dogs” of Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 7 recovered the crew using MH-60S Seahawk helos. Transit of USS Dwight D. Eisenhower off the East Coast. Source: MarineTraffic/KPLER (Reprinted with permission) Four shipboard personnel “were also injured during the mishap and are receiving medical care,” the Navy said. “One Sailor is being transported to a Norfolk-area hospital for treatment of non-life-threatening injuries,” according to the original statement. In total, eight sailors were evaluated by the ship’s medical team. The cause of the accident is still under investigation, and it’s unclear whether the aircraft was lost or if there was any damage to the carrier. TWZ has reached out to the Navy to find out more details. A Growler landing on the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower. U.S. Navy photo/Released Eisenhower wrapped an extended 15-month PIA earlier this year in April. The flattop had been pierside at Naval Station Norfolk since September 2 after being at sea for 12 days completing Fleet Replacement Squadron and Training Command Carrier Qualifications (CQ) in the Virginia Capes and Jacksonville operating areas. She got underway again on the afternoon of September 28, based on public AIS data, for Tailored Ship’s Training Availability, Final Evaluation Problem, and CQ, one of the final steps before onloading ammunition for COMPTUEX, where the full strike group certifies for deployment. Ike is working up in preparation for a future deployment scheduled for the first half of 2027, TWZ previously reported . Reports Surface That George H.W. Bush Is Headed To Thailand For A Port Call Multiple news outlets in Thailand reported Tuesday that USS George H.W. Bush and destroyer USS Delbert D. Black , which have both been in the Middle East in support of operations against Iran, will make a port call in Phuket in early October. If such a transit occurs, this would leave one carrier , the USS George Washington , on station in the U.S. 5th Fleet AOR for the first time since April . The Navy has not formally made an announcement, and TWZ has not verified the accounts. USS George H.W. Bush operating in CENTCOM. U.S. Navy photo Super Hornet on USS George H.W. Bush. U.S. Navy photo The reports are based on a meeting that representatives of the U.S. Embassy in Thailand allegedly held with the Patong police to discuss security protocols during the stop. “The visit has prompted coordination between Thai authorities and US officials over security, public order, and the movement of visiting military personnel during shore leave,” Phuket News wrote. According to the article, Patong police met with two deputy assistant defense attachés, Lou Pham and Robert Robinson, to discuss the visit. U.S. personnel were advised to comply with Thai laws during their stay, a specific request that may have been triggered by the recent visit of Lincoln . There are conflicting accounts of when Bush would arrive in Phuket’s deep-sea port, but the visit will likely last five or six days, which is similar to Lincoln’s recent port call in the Southeast Asian country. If the timeline holds, it means Bush is likely already en route from her station in the Arabian Sea, where the CSG was most recently operating as of September 25, according to DVIDS. The Bangko k Post and Thai Examiner also reported the upcoming visit. Notably, the reports do not mention any of the other warships that have been part of the Bush CSG in the past, including USS Donald Cook , USS Ross , USS Mason , or USS Princeton . The composition of the Bush CSG has shifted throughout the cruise. Big Deck Fleet At A Glance Overall, four U.S. carriers are deployed (with one heading home), three are working up in various states of readiness, three are in current or upcoming maintenance, one is being used primarily for training before deactivation next year, and the future USS John F. Kennedy , the second Ford class carrier, has received preliminary acceptance ahead of delivery in spring 2027. Two amphibious ready groups are deployed, one is forward-deployed, three are working up or in port, and three are in maintenance. Note: Positions are general approximations. Non-deployed LHA/LHD amphibious warships are not shown. Contact the author: ian@twz.com or @ianellisjones The post Where Are The Aircraft Carriers?: September 30, 2026 appeared first on TWZ .

title: Russia just accidentally crashed its first Tu-95 bomber in 11 years. Its missiles will keep striking Ukraine anyway
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A Russian Tu-95 bomber crashed on takeoff in Russia's Far East on Tuesday, the type's first crash in 11 years It's potentially the 11th Tu-95 the Russians have lost in the current wider war, and they can't build more But Russia still has enough bombers to keep up its missile raids on Ukraine A Russian air force Tupolev Tu-95 Bear bomber crashed on takeoff, apparently from Ukrainka air base in Amur Oblast in Russia's Far East. The Russian defense ministry said the plane was on a training flight without munitions and blamed a technical fault. The crash, while reportedly accidental, is still a win of sorts for Ukraine. Every bomber the Russians lose is a bomber they can't immediately replace—and sortie for missile strikes on Ukrainian cities. The problem for Ukraine is that Russia still has bombers to spare. It'll take more than a few crashes or drone raids on Russian bomber bases to cut into Russia's capacity to bombard Ukraine. That's why Ukraine needs missile-armed fighters , ground-based self-propelled guns, speedy interceptor drones , and long-range surface-to-air missiles such as American-made Patriots, among other air defenses. The Ukrainians can't prevent missile attacks by destroying bombers or waiting for bombers to crash; they need to shoot down missiles as they near their targets. A Russian Tu-95MS Bear heavy bomber crashed on takeoff in Amur this evening during a training flight. The airframe is a total loss, with no survivors reported. pic.twitter.com/tbujV6RVP5 — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) September 29, 2026 A security camera on the ground recorded a large aircraft plunging toward the ground in Amur Oblast on Tuesday night. Video from the crash site confirmed it was one of the Russians' four-engine, propeller-driven Tu-95s, aging workhorses in Russia's escalating campaign of missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities. The crash killed six crew and left one survivor injured, according to Russian state media. It is the first Tu-95 to go down in 11 years, Defense Express notes , and the first known non-combat loss of the type since the full-scale invasion. It's potentially the 11th Tu-95 Russia has lost since widening its war on Ukraine in February 2022. Ukrainian drones caught two Bears on the ground at Engels-2 air base in Saratov Oblast in July and August. On 1 June 2025, Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb—coordinated strikes on Russian bomber bases by more than 100 small drones smuggled across Russia in trucks—destroyed as many as four Bears at Olenya air base on the Kola Peninsula and another four at Belaya air base in Irkutsk Oblast. Now the Russian air force may be down to somewhere between 36 and 44 working Tu-95s, depending on the count, the youngest of which rolled out of the factory in the 1990s. That matters because the Tu-95 is, like the jet-propelled Tupolev Tu-22M bomber, out of production. Vendors have gone out of business. The skilled workers who assembled the types retired decades ago. While the Russians can still build one or two Tupolev Tu-160 jet bombers every year, slowly growing a fleet that currently stands at around 18 active planes, that's far too few new bombers to replace combat losses as the wider war grinds through its 56th month. On September 8, four Tu-95MS from Olenya Air Base and two Tu-160M from Ukrainka Air Base conducted a combat mission against Ukraine. The Tu-95MSs and Tu-160Ms launched Kh-101 cruise missiles from the airspace over the Leningrad and Smolensk oblasts. pic.twitter.com/xAZRc8EDO5 — AviVector (@avivector) September 8, 2026 Slow attrition The Russians have also lost at least nine Tu-22Ms, and possibly far more: Defense Express estimates losses at up to 70% of the combat-ready fleet since 2022. All told, Russia's bomber force has shrunk to around 105 planes since the wider war began, or fewer. Equally problematically for the Russians, the old Tu-95s and Tu-22Ms that carry out the majority of air-launched cruise missile strikes on Ukraine are wearing out from heavy use; not all are available for front-line use as more airframes spend more time in deep maintenance. Explore further Ukraine is working down the short list of ships that shell its cities with cruise missiles. A Neptune reached one of them tied up at its own pier But a Tu-95 carries as many as eight Kh-101 cruise missiles at a time; a Tu-22M carries up to three Kh-22s or Kh-32s. A Russian drone and missile strike might include just a dozen or so air-launched cruise missiles launched by a handful of bombers. A raid on 8 September involved just four Tu-95s and two Tu-160s. The Russians don't need 105 bombers to sustain six-bomber raids once or twice a week, even as those bombers suffer more and more wear and tear. Ukraine would have to take out a lot more Russian bombers, and fast, to put a dent in Russian strikes. Unless and until that unlikelihood happens, Ukraine will still need to defeat Russian raids inside Ukraine—by shooting down hundreds of incoming drones and missiles at a time. But that's getting harder as the Russians deploy faster jet-propelled Geran drones and more ground-launched Iskander missiles, combining them with the bomber-launched missiles in complex packages that routinely overwhelm ammunition-starved Ukrainian air defenses.

title: Ukraine’s F-16 Fleet Is In A Readiness Crisis
body: Ukraine’s F-16 fleet is facing growing pressure from the demands of the air war , with a shortage of air-to-air missiles now compounded by what appears to be a serious bottleneck in the critical maintenance system supporting the aging aircraft. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that more than half of Ukraine’s F-16s are currently in what a Western source described as “maintenance limbo.” The same source told the newspaper that, at the current rate of operations and maintenance, Ukraine could exhaust the remainder of its available aircraft by the end of the year. An F-16 over the Kyiv region on August 18, 2026. The jet carries four Sidewinder missiles, a Sniper targeting pod, and an AN/ALQ-131 electronic countermeasures pod. Photo by Roman PILIPEY / AFP ROMAN PILIPEY The Ukrainian Air Force declined to provide the WSJ with figures on the status of the fleet. Open-source analysis suggests that Ukraine may have received around 40-50 F-16s so far. However, a proportion of these are held back for training elsewhere in Europe , while there have been five confirmed losses . Approximately 110 F-16s have now been promised by a coalition comprising Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway. This is a growing issue, especially because right now F-16s are playing an important role in intercepts of jet powered Geran-4/5. https://t.co/ZtMFBSLAy1 — Michael Kofman (@KofmanMichael) September 30, 2026 The report follows TWZ ’s recent reporting on a separate constraint affecting the F-16 force: Ukraine is struggling to maintain adequate stocks of air-to-air missiles for its fighters. AIM-9 Sidewinders and AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles (AMRAAM) have been heavily used against Russian cruise missiles and drones, and Ukrainian F-16 pilots have reportedly had to ration their missile shots. Aircraft have increasingly had to rely on their internal 20mm cannon when suitable missiles are not available. This is a far from ideal substitute, as you can read about here , but Kyiv is reportedly now negotiating for tens of thousands of additional rounds of 20mm ammunition. The moment a Russian jet-powered "Shahed" drone is shot down by an F-16 fighter jet using its M61 Vulcan cannon. pic.twitter.com/gU72HJTXUa — WarTranslated (@wartranslated) September 23, 2026 Ukrainian F-16s have apparently been carrying laser-guided 70mm Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (APKWS II) rockets, which should provide an extremely valuable, lower-cost option for engaging long-range drones and subsonic cruise missiles. The exact status of this weapon in Ukrainian hands is unclear, but there is so far limited evidence of extensive use by its F-16s, at least in the public domain. All these problems are closely related because the same high operational tempo that is consuming Ukraine’s missile stocks is also putting additional hours on the already well-worn F-16 airframes. The aircraft have become a critical important component of Ukraine’s air-defense effort, particularly as Russia has expanded its use of increasingly sophisticated one-way attack drones, as we wrote about only yesterday. WSJ reports that Russia has launched around 2,000 jet-powered drones against Ukraine this month, compared with approximately 350 in June. The newer, jet-powered drones can reportedly reach speeds of up to 375 miles per hour, making them more difficult for Ukraine’s interceptor drones to engage and increasing the importance of conventional fighters. At the same time, the stocks of effectors for ground-based air defense systems are being reduced, in some cases to a critical level , increasing the reliance on crewed fighters to take up the slack. A Ukrainian drone attempts to intercept a Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drone. GUR F-16s are well-suited to the counter-drone and counter-cruise missile mission, but using them extensively against large numbers of relatively inexpensive targets presents a difficult sustainment problem. In fact, the lower speed and altitude differential between the F-16 and a jet-powered drone, compared to a propeller-driven one, makes the higher-performance weapon an easier target for the crewed fighter in most scenarios. However, every sortie adds flight hours to the aircraft, while each missile engagement draws from an inventory that Ukraine and its Western partners have to replenish. As the aircraft accumulate hours, they reach scheduled inspection and maintenance intervals, increasing demand on a maintenance network that is already supporting a fleet operating under wartime conditions. The United States has established a substantial support arrangement for that purpose. In January, the Pentagon awarded Belgian company Sabena Aerospace Engineering a contract with a ceiling of approximately $235.5 million for intermediate- and depot-level maintenance of Ukrainian F-16 aircraft and engines, together with associated material-management support. The contract runs through January 2029, with approximately $69.7 million initially obligated. Ukrainian Air Force F-16AM Fighting Falcon departing Belgium after receiving depot-level maintenance earlier this year. pic.twitter.com/Hy35iUZd8P — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) August 28, 2026 The contract provides an indication of the scale of the infrastructure required to keep the Ukrainian F-16 fleet operational. It also highlights why the reported turnaround times in Belgium are significant. A typical phase-inspection that would normally take approximately two to six weeks in the United States is reportedly taking as long as 40 weeks in Belgium. A 40-week turnaround does not necessarily mean that an aircraft spends 40 weeks continuously undergoing a phase inspection. The overall period an aircraft is unavailable can also include waiting for parts, additional repairs, scheduling, and other work. It is unclear exactly how many Ukrainian F-16s are currently affected by these various factors. U.S. Air Force engine shop where airmen remove the engine of an F-16 during a phase maintenance inspection in the United States. U.S. Air National Guard photo by Master Sgt. Christopher Stewart/Released Master Sgt. Christopher Stewart At the same time, the reported turnaround times do point to a substantial capacity problem. Ukraine operates a relatively small F-16 fleet, so aircraft that remain unavailable for extended periods have a disproportionate effect on the number of fighters that can actually be generated for combat missions. Its mission spectrum also includes air-to-ground sorties , putting more demand on the hard-pressed F-16 fleet. F-16 fighters are the best way to counter new Russian jet-powered drones. Ukrainian F-16 aces have shot down about 2,500 drones of all types and about 650 cruise missiles. Jet drones are exactly the kind of target F-16s shoot down very well, and it usually costs $25,000 or… pic.twitter.com/ajxYN9K0yK — Slava (@Heroiam_Slava) September 30, 2026 The F-16s have finite airframe lives, require increasingly substantial inspections as they accumulate hours, and depend on a supply chain for engines, components and other parts. The missiles used to destroy the targets are another finite resource. It should also be recalled that the jets supplied to Ukraine are among the oldest still in operational service. Although upgraded to F-16AM/BM standard, the airframes have accumulated a lot of hours and fatigue. There is an additional complication with the air-to-air missile inventory, too. AMRAAM is not used only by Ukrainian F-16s, but also employed by its NASAMS ground-based air-defense systems. Sidewinders, too, have both air-launched and surface-launched applications . The same broader Western supply chain therefore has to support both fighter operations and some of Ukraine’s surface-to-air missile systems. Stocks of both AMRAAM and Sidewinder have been eroded by Ukraine, as well as by combat actions in the Middle East . Southern Ukraine, a Ukrainian NASAMS surface to air missile system intercepts a Russian drone with an (SL)AIM-120B AMRAAM. pic.twitter.com/LTeDDHaECp — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) May 22, 2025 At the same time, Ukraine is continuing to receive additional F-16s. Belgium has said it will transfer three more aircraft to Ukraine before the end of this year. More aircraft will increase the potential size of the force, but they will also add to the requirement for spare parts, engines, technicians and depot capacity. “There is an important agreement ​with Belgium on the transfer of three F-16 ​fighter jets by the end of this year,” ⁠Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X. “We will work to receive ​these aircraft through an accelerated procedure.” There is an important agreement with Belgium on the transfer of three F-16 fighter jets by the end of this year. We will work to receive these aircraft through an accelerated procedure. We have already received urgent deliveries of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and other… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 29, 2026 Zelensky said Ukraine had ​already received “urgent deliveries” of F-16 weapons from Belgium and Spain, among other countries. The alternatives to the F-16 are also limited in the near term. Ukraine continues to operate the Soviet-era MiG-29 Fulcrum and a small number of Su-27 Flankers , but these aircraft are themselves aging and are also required for strike missions . In their favor, the Soviet types were designed around a different concept of operations, making them easier to maintain in the field, and Ukraine has its own support infrastructure to sustain them. The French Mirage 2000-5F force provides another Western option, but deliveries have been relatively limited, and additional aircraft are arriving incrementally rather than in numbers that can quickly compensate for a major reduction in F-16 availability. The longer-term fighter replacement plan is more ambitious. Sweden has agreed to provide 16 Gripen C/D fighters , with the first aircraft expected in early 2027, while a separate agreement covers the purchase of 16 new Gripen E fighters whose deliveries are not scheduled to begin until early 2029. French-delivered Dassault Mirage 2000-5F fighter jet in service of the Ukrainian Air Force during flight somewhere over Ukraine. pic.twitter.com/eBCjtx2Gjc — Status-6 (@Archer83Able) May 17, 2026 That leaves the F-16 as the principal Western fighter capability available to Ukraine for the immediate future, increasing the significance of any prolonged disruption to its maintenance pipeline or its supply of air-to-air weapons. Ukraine needs enough aircraft to maintain a meaningful combat presence, enough missiles to arm them for the missions they are being asked to fly, and enough maintenance capacity to keep those aircraft available as their flight hours accumulate. All this is becoming more important as Russia’s aerial campaign evolves. If the increase in faster jet-powered drones continues, Ukraine may have to devote still more fighter sorties to countering them at the very same time that a large portion of its existing F-16 fleet is reportedly unavailable and its stocks of air-to-air missiles are under serious pressure.
