title: F-15EX May Finally Get Missile Warning System The USAF Originally Skimped On Buying
body: The U.S. Air Force is looking at adding a missile warning system (MWS) to its new F-15EX Eagle II fighters . This will give the aircraft a way to optically detect incoming missile threats, especially passively guided ones like heat-seeking infrared-guided missiles, which they currently lack. The continued absence of an MWS has become more pronounced in light of recent combat experiences over Iran . The F-15EX is derived from earlier F-15 variants that all have MWSs, and it had seemed logical to expect the Eagle II would feature this capability . So it was puzzling when the first examples rolled out without such a system, and no apparent plans to install one on a jet already costing upwards of $100 million. The omission has been glaring for years now, especially given that the aircraft has all the provisions for such a system, including blanked-over spots for the sensors. The 22nd F-15EX for the US Air Force seen departing Boeing’s plant in St. Louis, Missouri, in August 2026. USAF/Senior Airman Melany Bermudez The Air Force has 22 Eagle IIs in inventory now and currently plans to acquire a total fleet of 267 of the jets. The aircraft’s manufacturer, Boeing, is on contract now to build 120 F-15EXs, including a lot of 22 jets through a new $2.38 billion deal also announced yesterday. Now, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s (AFLCMC) Fighters & Advanced Aircraft Directorate “is seeking sources for the procurement of an operationally qualified threat missile launch and approach warning system for rapid integration into the United States Air Force (USAF) F-15EX Eagle II fighter aircraft,” per a contracting notice put out yesterday. “The MWS must alert the F-15EX aircrew to the presence of missiles that may threaten the aircraft without unreasonably distracting the aircrew with false alarms.” As mentioned, the F-15EX is already configured to accommodate an MWS, inside and out, something AFLCMC’s notice emphasizes. This is a result of the Eagle II having been directly derived from the F-15QA variant for Qatar , which itself was an outgrowth of the F-15SA for Saudi Arabia . While many of the F-15EX’s advances come from these aircraft, the first F-15 variant to get an MWS was actually Singapore’s F-15SG . The Advanced Eagle line and the F-15SG are part of Boeing’s extended F-15E Strike Eagle family . A pair of Qatari F-15QA Advanced Eagles. USAF “The MWS must use the six (6) pre-existing F-15EX sensor locations, data cables, power cables, and cooling,” the contracting notice says. “It must be easily, safely, rapidly, and organically installable and removable in the field by USAF military aircraft maintenance personnel without requiring any change to aircraft configuration beyond installation of MWS line replaceable units (LRUs) in the six (6) pre-existing locations in the aircraft dedicated for missile warning.” The most visually prominent of those pre-existing sensor locations are two horn-like sponsons, one on each side of the forward fuselage right below the cockpit canopy. There are two more locations at the ends of the jet’s tail booms. The last two locations are situated so additional sensors can face straight up and down to provide total 360-degree coverage. A closer look at the nose end of an F-15EX, with the right-side horn-like sponson under the cockpit plainly visible. USAF/Master Sgt. Steph Sawyer The F-15EX also has pre-existing locations for MWS sensors at the ends of its tailplanes, as can be seen in this picture. USAF The sources sought notice does not mention any specific MWS and invites prospective vendors to submit proposals. It also stresses that the Air Force is still in the “market research” phase of the contracting process and that it “does not constitute [a] solicitation and shall not be construed as a commitment” to buy such a system. The F-15SA uses the AN/AAR-57 Common Missile Warning System (CMWS), and this system is understood to also be found on the F-15QA. Beyond F-15 variants, versions of the AN/AAR-57, for which BAE Systems is currently the prime contractor, are fielded today on a wide variety of other fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters, including various types in U.S. military service. CMWS variants are notably found across the U.S. Army’s AH-64, UH-60, and CH-47 helicopter fleets. A picture of a Saudi Arabian F-15SA Advanced Eagle. Jamie Hunter Another close-up look at a Saudi F-15SA, offering a particularly good view of one of the aircraft’s missile warning sensors. USAF/Staff Sgt. Isaiah Soliz All versions of the CMWS consist of several electro-optic missile sensors (EOMS), the number of which varies from platform to platform, linked to a central electronic control unit (ECU). The system is also designed to be integrated into larger defensive suites. A picture showing five of the electro-optic missile sensors (EOMS) used in the AN/AAR-57, as well as the electronic control unit. BAE Systems While the AN/AAR-57 is a proven system with years of successful integration on the F-15 and other platforms, it is just one option of the open market today. The Air Force could choose to take another route, possibly with a new system that offers added functionality . The addition of any MWS will give the F-15EX a valuable, if not increasingly critical, boost in defensive capability. The Eagle II does already have an extremely powerful self-protection suite, including the Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System (EPAWSS). However, it is heavily geared toward defending against radar-based threats that pump out signals that can be detected and jammed. Infrared-homing anti-air missiles zero in on their targets passively. In general, MWSs also typically make use of passive infrared sensors to spot the heat plumes of missile launches and the thermal signatures of those threats as they continue their approach. BAE Systems says current-generation versions of the AN/AAR-57 are sensitive enough to detect infantry anti-armor rockets being launched , as well as small arms fire from the ground, under the right circumstances. Though an MWS is not an active countermeasure unto itself, the early warning it provides gives critical time to deploy flares or employ other defensive capabilities, or just take evasive action. TWZ touched on all of this last month after The New York Times reported new details about the shootdown of an F-15E Strike Eagle over Iran in April. A shoulder-fired, heat-seeking surface-to-air missile, also known as a man-portable air defense system (MANPADS), is said to have been responsible, though this remains unconfirmed. The Strike Eagle also lacks an MWS. The Times ‘ story said that the F-15E’s defensive suite provided the crew with only half a second of warning. As we noted at the time , it would actually have provided no warning given that the Strike Eagle also lacks an MWS. A picture showing one of the tailfins of the F-15E shot down over Iran in April 2026. Iranian state media Even before the current conflict with Iran broke out, TWZ had questioned the F-15EX’s lack of this capability given the general focus on increased survivability to match expanding threat ecosystems globally . EPAWSS is already a reflection of that reality, and could be made even more capable when tied together with an MWS. In May, we had reached out to the Air Force about any plans to integrate an MWS onto the F-15EX in light of observations from the ongoing conflict with Iran. The service told us then that it had no details to share. Whether the service now has any plans to add MWSs to the Strike Eagle fleet, which would require more significant integration work, is also unknown. Buying F-15EX and not springing for the missile approach warning system is absolutely the dumbest thing. $100M fighter, but let's save a few bucks on a key defensive advantage. You are not always going to get a radar spike from a threat, even at altitude. — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) April 4, 2026 They also didn't buy conformals for the first EXs. So silly. — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) April 4, 2026 Infrared homing anti-air missiles, as well as air defense systems that use passive infrared sensors for target detection and cueing, are certainly not threats limited to Iran. In Yemen, Iranian-backed Houthi militants have been making good use of these capabilities for years now, something else we have explored in great detail in the past . The Houthis claimed to have downed a Saudi Arabian F-15 just earlier this month and, per a now-long standing modus operandi, subsequently released video captured through a ground-based forward-looking infrared (FLIR) system as evidence. The group also shared images of the wreckage of what looked to be an F-15SA Advanced Eagle , underscoring the dangers posed even to aircraft equipped MWSs. Onboard footage of a Houthi SAM system shooting down a Saudi F-15 overnight over Yemen’s Marib province. pic.twitter.com/6mh23B2Ovu — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) September 16, 2026 These threats are not limited to the Middle East more broadly, either, and are only increasingly likely to be encountered in future conflicts globally. The emergence of ever-more capable and longer-range anti-air missiles with infrared or dual-mode guidance systems is a significant factor in all this. Expanding use of passive infrared search and track (IRST) systems on aircraft and infrared sensors on ground-based air defense systems are part of this larger equation , as well. How the Air Force ultimately decided to proceed with the integration of an MWS onto the F-15EX fleet remains to be seen. However, the Eagle II’s lack of this capability is only becoming more striking, especially in light of the conflict with Iran. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post F-15EX May Finally Get Missile Warning System The USAF Originally Skimped On Buying appeared first on TWZ .

title: Operation Atlantic City ushers Marines on rare trip to ... remote Arctic island
body: U.S. Marines participated in a “first-of-its-kind mission” in the remote Arctic this summer, meant to test their ability to work with Norwegian and British troops in harsh conditions. The operation — on the far-flung and strategically valuable island of Jan Mayen, Norway — reflects NATO’s increasing focus on the Arctic, where the alliance is worried about Russia’s ability to project power and disrupt critical infrastructure. The exercise also gave Marines a chance to practice defending “key maritime terrain” with tactics they refined in the Pacific. Dubbed Operation Atlantic City, a reference to a WWII-era U.S. base on Jan Mayen, the Norwegian-led exercise ran from Aug. 26 to Sept. 4 and marked the first instance of “rapid insertion of military assets to remote and austere locations,” the Marine Corps said. A news release described the exercise as focused on developing expeditionary advanced basing capabilities and on testing participants’ ability to conduct combined fires missions, provide maritime domain awareness and deny adversaries the use of nearby sea lanes. It was a demonstration of the militaries’ ability to “integrate multinational sensors, command-and-control nodes, and precision fires into a unified, joint kill web.” Training with weapons that could challenge enemy air and naval movements appeared to be a major element. At the start of the exercise, a U.S. Air Force C-17 transported a U.S. Navy Containerized Launching System — a 40-foot container with four launch cells for anti-air and anti-ship missiles — to Trondheim in central Norway in a strategic airlift mission to demonstrate “rapid projection of joint logistics and interoperable communication assets.” U.S. and British cargo aircraft also transported vehicles and equipment — including U.S. Joint Light Tactical Vehicles, a Norwegian National Maneuver Air Defense System, and an Australian Strikemaster anti-ship-missile system operated by Marines — to Jan Mayen as part of the rapid-insertion training. The vehicles were moved around the island to test troops’ ability to position and protect assets on rough and contested territory. Those platforms were also employed to relay targeting data and communications as part of what the Corps calls “a resilient kill web” comprising dispersed weapons and command-and-control nodes. Other drills, like the delivery of medical supplies using an aerial drone, underscored the exercise’s expeditionary focus. Holding ‘key maritime terrain’ at risk A mountainous island 620 miles from mainland Norway with an active volcano and partially covered by glaciers, Jan Mayen is uninhabited except for a few dozen Norwegian military personnel and Norwegian Meteorological Institute staff. But it is a strategic outpost in waters “vital to NATO in terms of securing international sea lines of communication and transatlantic supply routes,” a Norwegian official said after Operation Atlantic City 2025. The 2025 version of the exercise was the first time Marines operated on Jan Mayen, according to Lt. Col. Kurt Stahl, communications director for US Marine Corps Forces Europe. That came after an apparent lull in U.S. activity there since late 2019, when airmen visited to do an airfield assessment. This year’s Atlantic City was “quite significant” because it was the second consecutive year Marines ventured to the island, Stahl added. Jan Mayen provides a “true austere island location” where Marines can train on inhospitable but important terrain, said Lt. Col. David Palacio, fires officer for Marine Corps Forces Europe. “This year it was absolutely an integrated force, whether that was in targeting, intelligence, communications, also medical capabilities, which will be a concern in any type of austere and isolated environment like this,” Palacio said in a video released after the exercise, adding that troops were “really integrating significantly more than last year.” Atlantic City 2026’s content and location were reminiscent of Marine Corps exercises with allies in the Western Pacific. Over the past several years, Marines have deployed to Philippine and Japanese islands with sensors and weapons — notably the NMESIS anti-ship missile — that would allow them to monitor and control sea lanes and airspace around Taiwan that China would need to use in a conflict. Atlantic City 2026 was meant to ensure Marines in Europe could do similar tasks. The Joint Light Tactical Vehicle delivered to the island on a British cargo plane “was really being used as a surrogate for” NMESIS, Palacio said in another video. “So we were validating that this vehicle can fit on this aircraft and can be delivered rapidly to this location, which we did flawlessly.” The message of Atlantic City 2026 was also similar to that of the exercises on Japan’s southwest islands and in the northern Philippines: “It’s important for the adversary to know that, ‘Hey, this is a thing out here as well, too, so you’re not going to get sanctuary in areas that you thought,’” Palacio said. “‘That key maritime terrain that you thought you could just bypass? You now have to understand that you’re being held at risk.’” Approaching Russia’s ‘bastion’ Atlantic City 2026 also reflects NATO’s shift toward the Arctic. The exercise ran concurrently with Northern Viking, a NATO exercise focused on defending Iceland and sea lanes between Greenland, Iceland, and the UK — a chokepoint known as the GIUK Gap — and was part of NATO’s new Arctic Sentry initiative, which is a response to “Russia’s increasing military activity and China’s growing interest in the Arctic,” the alliance said. “Over the last three, four, five years, allied activity in the Arctic has more than doubled, so there’s a lot of interest in the Arctic,” Maj. Gen. Øivind Gunnerud, chief of the Royal Norwegian Air Force, said during an event at Norway’s embassy in Washington, D.C., in mid-September. Russia “is the most important military factor shaping our planning in the High North. It retains strategic, significant capabilities close to Norway,” including the powerful Northern Fleet, long-range aviation forces and advanced air and missile systems, Gunnerud said. NATO also has growing concerns about Moscow’s ability to disrupt critical infrastructure, particularly undersea data cables, in the Arctic and North Atlantic. NATO used the GIUK Gap as a vantage point to track Soviet submarines during the Cold War, and Moscow’s investment in its submarine force over the past two decades has given the chokepoint new relevance, but the interest in Jan Mayen is a sign that the alliance’s focus is moving farther north — closer to the Barents Sea, a “bastion” from which Russian subs could potentially strike targets in Europe with conventional and nuclear-armed missiles. Norway has led the way amid NATO’s shift to the north. In the coming years, the country will field new coast guard vessels designed for the Arctic, as well as new frigates and submarines. Paired with P-8 patrol planes that are already “flying constantly,” those ships will help in the “cat-and-mouse game up there to keep track of the submarines,” Gunnerud said. Norway is also investing more in Jan Mayen. Even before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Oslo invited allies to visit the island, and since then it has made plans to bolster its military posture and authority on the island. A planned undersea-cable project will also improve connectivity with mainland Norway. “Norway has unquestionably escalated” its presence on and funding to Jan Mayen, wrote Klaus Dodds and Caroline Kennedy-Pipe, professors and Arctic security experts, in a recent report for the Royal United Services Institute. “This was in part brought about in response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and it has seen a distinct change in the character of presence on the island,” they added. “From its long-standing duties as a meteorological outpost, it is now a crucial site of Norwegian security activity.”

It was a demonstration of the militaries’ ability to “integrate multinational sensors, command-and-control nodes, and precision fires into a unified, joint kill web.” Training with weapons that could challenge enemy air and naval movements appeared to be a major element. At the start of the exercise, a U.S. Air Force C-17 transported a U.S. Navy Containerized Launching System — a 40-foot container with four launch cells for anti-air and anti-ship missiles — to Trondheim in central Norway in a strategic airlift mission to demonstrate “rapid projection of joint logistics and interoperable communication assets.” U.S. and British cargo aircraft also transported vehicles and equipment — including U.S. Joint Light Tactical Vehicles, a Norwegian National Maneuver Air Defense System, and an Australian Strikemaster anti-ship-missile system operated by Marines — to Jan Mayen as part of the rapid-insertion training. The vehicles were moved around the island to test troops’ ability to position and protect assets on rough and contested territory. Those platforms were also employed to relay targeting data and communications as part of what the Corps calls “a resilient kill web” comprising dispersed weapons and command-and-control nodes. Other drills, like the delivery of medical supplies using an aerial drone, underscored the exercise’s expeditionary focus. Holding ‘key maritime terrain’ at risk A mountainous island 620 miles from mainland Norway with an active volcano and partially covered by glaciers, Jan Mayen is uninhabited except for a few dozen Norwegian military personnel and Norwegian Meteorological Institute staff. But it is a strategic outpost in waters “vital to NATO in terms of securing international sea lines of communication and transatlantic supply routes,” a Norwegian official said after Operation Atlantic City 2025. The 2025 version of the exercise was the first time Marines operated on Jan Mayen, according to Lt. Col. Kurt Stahl, communications director for US Marine Corps Forces Europe. That came after an apparent lull in U.S. activity there since late 2019, when airmen visited to do an airfield assessment. This year’s Atlantic City was “quite significant” because it was the second consecutive year Marines ventured to the island, Stahl added. Jan Mayen provides a “true austere island location” where Marines can train on inhospitable but important terrain, said Lt. Col. David Palacio, fires officer for Marine Corps Forces Europe. “This year it was absolutely an integrated force, whether that was in targeting, intelligence, communications, also medical capabilities, which will be a concern in any type of austere and isolated environment like this,” Palacio said in a video released after the exercise, adding that troops were “really integrating significantly more than last year.” Atlantic City 2026’s content and location were reminiscent of Marine Corps exercises with allies in the Western Pacific. Over the past several years, Marines have deployed to Philippine and Japanese islands with sensors and weapons — notably the NMESIS anti-ship missile — that would allow them to monitor and control sea lanes and airspace around Taiwan that China would need to use in a conflict. Atlantic City 2026 was meant to ensure Marines in Europe could do similar tasks. The Joint Light Tactical Vehicle delivered to the island on a British cargo plane “was really being used as a surrogate for” NMESIS, Palacio said in another video. “So we were validating that this vehicle can fit on this aircraft and can be delivered rapidly to this location, which we did flawlessly.” The message of Atlantic City 2026 was also similar to that of the exercises on Japan’s southwest islands and in the northern Philippines: “It’s important for the adversary to know that, ‘Hey, this is a thing out here as well, too, so you’re not going to get sanctuary in areas that you thought,’” Palacio said. “‘That key maritime terrain that you thought you could just bypass? You now have to understand that you’re being held at risk.’” Approaching Russia’s ‘bastion’ Atlantic City 2026 also reflects NATO’s shift toward the Arctic. The exercise ran concurrently with Northern Viking, a NATO exercise focused on defending Iceland and sea lanes between Greenland, Iceland, and the UK — a chokepoint known as the GIUK Gap — and was part of NATO’s new Arctic Sentry initiative, which is a response to “Russia’s increasing military activity and China’s growing interest in the Arctic,” the alliance said. “Over the last three, four, five years, allied activity in the Arctic has more than doubled, so there’s a lot of interest in the Arctic,” Maj. Gen. Øivind Gunnerud, chief of the Royal Norwegian Air Force, said during an event at Norway’s embassy in Washington, D.C., in mid-September. Russia “is the most important military factor shaping our planning in the High North. It retains strategic, significant capabilities close to Norway,” including the powerful Northern Fleet, long-range aviation forces and advanced air and missile systems, Gunnerud said. NATO also has growing concerns about Moscow’s ability to disrupt critical infrastructure, particularly undersea data cables, in the Arctic and North Atlantic. NATO used the GIUK Gap as a vantage point to track Soviet submarines during the Cold War, and Moscow’s investment in its submarine force over the past two decades has given the chokepoint new relevance, but the interest in Jan Mayen is a sign that the alliance’s focus is moving farther north — closer to the Barents Sea, a “bastion” from which Russian subs could potentially strike targets in Europe with conventional and nuclear-armed missiles. Norway has led the way amid NATO’s shift to the north. In the coming years, the country will field new coast guard vessels designed for the Arctic, as well as new frigates and submarines. Paired with P-8 patrol planes that are already “flying constantly,” those ships will help in the “cat-and-mouse game up there to keep track of the submarines,” Gunnerud said. Norway is also investing more in Jan Mayen. Even before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Oslo invited allies to visit the island, and since then it has made plans to bolster its military posture and authority on the island. A planned undersea-cable project will also improve connectivity with mainland Norway. “Norway has unquestionably escalated” its presence on and funding to Jan Mayen, wrote Klaus Dodds and Caroline Kennedy-Pipe, professors and Arctic security experts, in a recent report for the Royal United Services Institute. “This was in part brought about in response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and it has seen a distinct change in the character of presence on the island,” they added. “From its long-standing duties as a meteorological outpost, it is now a crucial site of Norwegian security activity.”

title: Greece Assumes UN Security Council Presidency As Of Today
body: Greece assumes the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council as of October 1, beginning its second and final month in the role during its 2025-26 term as an elected member. Greece previously held the presidency in May 2025, while its two-year term on the 15-member Security Council ends on December 31. Greece’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Aglaia Balta, will preside over the council’s work during October. The UN’s own schedule confirms Greece as the council’s October president. The presidency comes as the council faces several major international crises, deep divisions among its permanent members and repeated difficulties in reaching common responses to conflicts. The rotating presidency does not give Greece unilateral control over the council’s decisions or policies. Instead, the president chairs meetings and closed consultations, represents the council and manages its programme of work and day-to-day operations under the authority of all 15 members. Ukraine remains a major focus The war in Ukraine remains among the most pressing issues on the council’s agenda. At a high-level Security Council meeting on September 23, UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peace building Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo warned that the war had entered a “dangerous new phase”, with intensifying attacks, rising civilian casualties and increasing risks of regional spillover. UN figures show that 2,222 civilians died and 13,058 suffered injuries in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026. The combined figure exceeded the number of civilian casualties recorded throughout 2025. The UN has also warned about growing risks to energy infrastructure ahead of winter, cross-border incidents and military activity around nuclear facilities. Gaza and the Middle East The Middle East will also remain a major item for the council. In Gaza, the UN continues to describe the ceasefire as fragile, while Israeli strikes, humanitarian difficulties and the economic crisis continue to affect the territory. The council also faces the implementation of Resolution 2803 concerning transitional arrangements and the recovery of Gaza. In the West Bank, the UN has reported increased violence, settlement expansion, displacement and a severe fiscal crisis affecting the Palestinian Authority. Iran and the Strait of Hormuz The crisis surrounding Iran and the Strait of Hormuz could also demand particular attention during Greece’s presidency. On September 30, Tehran confirmed that Qatar had delivered the US response to Iran’s latest proposal for de-escalation, with the reopening of the Strait and restoration of normal shipping among the issues under discussion. The negotiations remain difficult, while the Security Council also faces questions surrounding sanctions reinstated in 2025 and overseen by the council’s 1737 Committee. The combination of Iran’s nuclear programme, sanctions, regional security and freedom of navigation makes the issue particularly complex for the council. Sudan and Haiti remain on the agenda Other conflicts will continue to require Security Council attention. In Sudan, fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces continues, alongside an increase in drone attacks. In Haiti, armed violence has displaced almost 1.5 million people. On September 29, the Security Council renewed for six months the mandate of the international force supporting efforts against armed gangs, ahead of elections scheduled for December. UN secretary-general race adds further significance October could also carry particular institutional significance because of the selection process for the next UN secretary-general. The Security Council is central to the process. In the fourth informal straw poll on September 29, Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan reportedly received 10 votes indicating “encouragement”, three indicating “discouragement” and two members expressing “no opinion”. The process continues, with no final consensus yet established. Under Article 97 of the UN Charter, the General Assembly appoints the secretary-general following a recommendation from the Security Council. Any recommendation therefore requires agreement within the council and cannot proceed if a permanent member blocks it with a veto. If the council reaches agreement during October, the recommendation could therefore emerge while Greece holds the presidency. A demanding final month Greece’s final month as Security Council president comes at a time when the body faces wars and international crises with consequences well beyond their immediate regions. For Greek diplomacy, the presidency will centre on managing the council’s procedures, facilitating communication among its 15 members and keeping its work functioning despite continuing geopolitical divisions. title: Ukraine is downing Russia’s fastest drones—just not often enough, and scaling up comes down to money

Each tool has limits, and the new interceptors still bring down only the occasional jet drone. The bottleneck now is money and factory output, not ideas. Russia is pouring faster jet-powered drones into the air war as winter nears, a campaign Western analysts say is meant to wear Ukraine's defenses down—and holding those skies now turns on which side can keep out-producing the other's cheap weapons. Fighter jets help, but they run on imported rounds Electronic jamming can work against some of the drones, and Ukraine is also sending combat aircraft up after them. But aviation has a catch: the jets need air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds, and for the F-16 and Mirage those are imported and not always in stock. Flying over Kyiv adds danger to the civilians below and to the pilots, so Ukraine would rather catch the drones out on the approaches. New interceptors are landing hits—just not enough The newest piece is a wave of Ukrainian interceptor drones built to chase the jet versions, which fly three times faster than the propeller Shaheds. Ukrainian crews have been downing the jet Gerans in a recent run: on 19 September, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, confirmed one Geran-5 shot down, and in late September, operators of the National Guard's Separate Artillery Brigade brought down a Geran-4 with the Bullet interceptor made by General Cherry, the first Geran-4 that drone has downed, Ukraine's National Association of Defense Industries said . Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said several prototypes have proven themselves in combat. Explore further Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest Across all methods, Ukraine now intercepts about 57% of the jet drones Russia launches, Zelenskyy said on 28 September—a rate that has climbed but still trails the 90%-plus it manages against slower Shaheds. Kills by the new interceptors specifically remain isolated. In August, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said jet drones can make up as much as two-thirds of the drones in some raids—though not every time. One promising route is reworking Ukraine's own long-range strike drones into interceptors. Kyiv is in talks with partners over the money; on 28 September, Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara asked the EU to help finance the interceptors so enough reach the front quickly. Hitting the launch sites and jamming the controls Ukrainian forces strike the Russian airfields the jet drones launch from, RBC-Ukraine's sources said, though the raids have not forced Russia to abandon the attacks. On 20 August, military intelligence hit drone storage and launch sites at Primorsko-Akhtarsk, one of the launch bases RBC names, and at occupied Donetsk airfield. Ukraine also keeps going after the Belarusian relay towers Russia strings into a mesh network to steer the drones in, RBC's sources said. title: The US has until 18 October to choose its Russia sanctions targets—if any. Kyiv’s wish list leads with the firms feeding Russia’s Starlink clone
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine is about to tell Washington exactly which Russian targets it wants punished under America's new sanctions law, the Associated Press reported . A senior Ukrainian diplomat said Kyiv will hand the Trump administration and Congress a wish list of companies, ships, and people this week—and at the top are the firms supplying parts for Russia's answer to Starlink. The law requires Washington to act but lets the president waive the sanctions if he certifies that doing so serves US national interests, and the first choice falls due in weeks. For Ukraine, a measure that names no targets changes nothing on the ground—which is why the fight now is over whose names make the list before the clock runs out. A list topped by Russia's Starlink clone Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said the priority is a group of Russian firms making components for Rassvet, Moscow's homegrown satellite network, which Russia hopes to complete by the end of the year—though its own officials have put the start of service in 2027. Bureau 1440, the firm building Rassvet, is not itself on US sanctions lists, but its parent company, ICS Holding, is under US blocking sanctions, according to Militarnyi. The suppliers feeding the network parts are not sanctioned, and those are the ones Kyiv wants added to the list. Russia sped up the project after Ukraine and SpaceX cut off the Starlink terminals its troops had used without authorization at the front. If Russia completes the constellation, Sienik said, it could strike Ukraine at will with real-time information—a danger he warned would bite hardest this winter. "If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this program possible for Russia and that will be a game-changer," he told reporters, Reuters reported. Kyiv wants access to Starlink inside Russia, too, so it can strike targets there. Euromaidan Press has reported how such a network would change the battlefield: the satellites transmit in high-frequency bands that are hard to jam, and a relay overhead would feed drones and missiles fresh coordinates mid-flight, letting them fly low under air defenses that struggle to see them. Oil tankers and attacks on US firms Ukraine is pushing for tougher action against Russia's shadow fleet, too—the aging tankers that sell its oil around Western restrictions —and is asking the administration and American industry to publicly condemn Russian attacks on US companies' operations inside Ukraine, Sienik said. The deadline Washington is now facing The requests arrive as the administration faces an 18 October deadline to decide which Russian entities, if any, to sanction under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act , which US President Donald Trump signed into law on 18 September. The law directs the White House to impose tariffs on Russia's biggest oil buyers and to block its banks, officials, and tankers—but lets the president waive those measures, which is why Kyiv is lobbying for the toughest list it can get. title: Cyprus Independence Day parade showcases Greek F-16s, Barak MX and foreign troops
body: NICOSIA: Cyprus marked the 66th anniversary of the Republic with a major military parade in Nicosia featuring Greek F-16 Vipers, the first public appearance of the Israeli-made Barak MX air defence system and military contingents from the United States, France, Britain and Egypt. The parade on October 1 also showcased new unmanned systems being developed and operated by the Cyprus National Guard, alongside armoured vehicles, artillery and other newly introduced capabilities. Greek F-16s over Nicosia Two Hellenic Air Force F-16 Viper fighter jets made a low pass over Nicosia during the parade, highlighting Greece’s military presence at the Republic’s Independence Day celebrations. Greek F-16 Vipers roar over Nicosia! Two Hellenic Air Force F-16 Vipers made a low pass over the Cypriot capital during today’s Cyprus Independence Day military parade. A powerful Greek presence in the skies over Cyprus. #Cyprus #Greece #F16 #IndependenceDay pic.twitter.com/5VClhkkzIx — Greek City Times (@greekcitytimes) October 1, 2026 The aircraft had conducted a rehearsal flight over the Cypriot capital earlier in the week ahead of Thursday’s parade. Greece was also represented at the highest level, with Defence Minister Nikos Dendias and Chief of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff General Dimitrios Houpis attending alongside Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides and Cypriot Defence Minister Vasilis Palmas. Barak MX makes first public appearance One of the major highlights was the first public display of the Barak MX air defence system , recently incorporated into the Cyprus National Guard. The Israeli-developed system was presented alongside other new weapons and military equipment during the mechanised section of the parade. Barak MX Multiple rocket launchers, including the Tamnava , were also displayed, while the National Guard presented its Poseidon H-10 unmanned aircraft , which have been incorporated into its artillery capabilities. Drones and unmanned systems featured prominently throughout the parade, reflecting the growing role of unmanned technology in Cyprus’ military planning. Three specialised vehicles designed to support FPV drone operations were also presented for the first time. Two are designed to transport and support small drones used for surveillance, reconnaissance and strike missions, while another operates as a mobile workshop for the construction and technical support of unmanned aircraft. Cypriot defence industry companies have also been involved in developing these capabilities. The National Guard’s newly established Chemical, Biological and Radiological Threat Response Platoon also took part in the parade. ELDYK takes part with armoured vehicles For the first time, units of the Hellenic Force in Cyprus (ELDYK) participated with mechanised assets. The Greek contingent displayed LEONIDAS armoured vehicles , Hummer vehicles equipped with KORNET-E anti-tank missiles and M-106 armoured mortar carriers . The parade also featured commandos, reservists, naval and air force units, the National Guard, military academy cadets and personnel from the Cyprus Police, Fire Service, Civil Defence, Ambulance Service and Forestry Department. US, French, British and Egyptian troops Another notable feature was the participation of foreign military contingents from four countries. The United States was represented by 17 Marines from the USS Roosevelt , while France sent a contingent of 22 Marines. Britain participated with a military band and marching contingent, while Egypt was represented by military police personnel and an infantry contingent. An Egyptian C-295 transport aircraft also took part in the aerial component of the celebrations. Among the senior foreign military officials attending was the UK Chief of the Defence Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton , along with representatives of the armed forces of Egypt, France and the United States. Greek frigate in Larnaca The Independence Day celebrations extended beyond Nicosia. In the port of Larnaca, the Cyprus National Guard offshore patrol vessel Ioannidis was joined by the Hellenic Navy frigate HS Nikiforos Fokas . The day’s commemorations began with a memorial service and wreath-laying ceremony at the Imprisoned Graves, followed by ceremonies at the Presidential Palace and the Monument of Democracy and Resistance. The October 1 parade once again placed Cyprus’ defence capabilities and its expanding military partnerships at the centre of the Republic’s Independence Day celebrations. title: Bristling with steel spikes and guarded by a bomber drone, two Ukrainian tanks charged Russian infiltrators and lived to tell the tale
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); The 475th Assault Regiment found a new way to protect its tanks from Russian drones It surrounded its up-armored tanks with drones of its own During a recent counter-infiltration mission, two 475th Assault Regiment tanks were shepherded into battle by three different drone types Russian infiltrators have been slipping into villages and towns along Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia, likely aiming to draw Ukrainian troops away from the bigger fights farther south around the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Desperate to clear out the infiltrators without dedicating too many precious infantry to the task, the Ukrainian 475th Assault Regiment formed a unique team: two heavily up-armored tanks plus three different types of drone. The drones scouted ahead of the tanks and protected them as they trundled through Russia's own drone kill zone on their way to a point-blank clash with Russian troops. In this mission, the blend of mechanized and unmanned forces worked: the tanks accomplished their mission and survived to fight another day. If the tank-drone pairing keeps working, expect it to become more common all along the 1,200-km gray zone as Ukraine struggles with a deepening shortage of manpower. Two Ukrainian turtle tanks of Code 9.2 of the 475 Assault Regiment assault Russian position in Vilkhuvatka, Kharkiv Oblast @GeoConfirmed @UAControlMap 50.187782, 37.508585 src: https://t.co/ItVhiR0hrW pic.twitter.com/4KlQZaYt0T — Bielitz (@Bielitzling) September 30, 2026 It's unclear what kinds of tanks the 475th Assault Regiment operates. It is clear how the regiment protects the tanks from ever-present Russian drones. The unit wraps the tanks in metal cages and then welds hundreds of metal spines on the cages. The spines trigger incoming explosive drones at a safe distance from the tank's hull. The cage supports the spines and catches any drones the spines may miss. We call these kinds of tanks "hedgehog tanks." The Russians developed the hedgehog application but, seeing that it worked, deflecting potentially dozens of drones at a time, the Ukrainians copied it. Hedgehog helpers But even the best-protected hedgehog tank might struggle to get through the enemy's kill zone when that kill zone may include bomber and one-way attack drones in the air and loitering ambush drones waiting on the ground as well as mines and other threats. Sometimes the best defense against a drone is another drone, and the 475th Assault Regiment put that truism into practice. To shepherd those two hedgehog tanks into battle with Russian infiltrators in the village of Vilkhuvatka, in Kharkiv Oblast 9 km from the border with Russia, the regiment deployed a Vampire heavy bomber drone, at least one explosive first-person-view (FPV) quadcopter, and at least one surveillance quadcopter. Vilkhuvatka on a map (Euromaidan Press) The surveillance drones could scout ahead. The bomber drone could blast mines and loitering ambush drones. The FPVs could intercept incoming enemy FPVs. The layered protection was effective. As evident in the 475th Assault Regiment's video depicting the two-tank counter-assault, the tanks took multiple hits from Russian drones and mines, but not enough hits to slow them down. Explore further Russia may soon have more tanks than pre-war. It just can’t use them. Both tanks reached an intersection inside Vilkhuvatka, fired their cannons at nearby Russian infiltrators, and then withdrew. It should come as no surprise that the 475th Assault Regiment is pioneering mixed formations of drones and tanks. The regiment recently partnered with the 1st Assault Regiment to develop new "multi-domain" tactics combining ground, air, and cyber forces. "We came to the conclusion that fighting in only one domain makes no sense," said "Perun," the 1st Assault Regiment commander. "We'd simply lose because the enemy would bring another domain into play." The key takeaway is that, despite the serious threat that drones and mines pose to tanks in the fifth year of Russia's wider war on Ukraine, tanks can still fight, win, and survive—if they have plenty of support from the same kinds of drones that, in enemy hands, vex them along every kilometer of disputed terrain. The tank isn't dead yet. It just needs a little help.
